question:
A 53-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 1-month history of cough productive of small amounts of blood-tinged sputum. During this time, he has also developed fatigue, myalgia, and shortness of breath on exertion. He has had a 4-lb (2-kg) weight loss over the past 2 months. He has no personal history of serious illness. His mother has systemic lupus erythematosus. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 152/98 mm Hg. Diffuse rhonchi are heard on auscultation of the chest bilaterally. There are multiple palpable, erythematous, nonblanching lesions on the lower extremities bilaterally. Laboratory studies show:
Leukocyte count 12,300 cells/mm3
Platelet count 400,000 cells/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 83 mm/hr
Serum
Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL
Antinuclear antibody 1:40
Urine
Protein 3+
Blood 2+
RBC casts numerous
A biopsy specimen of the skin shows inflammation of the arterioles and capillaries without granuloma formation. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Symptoms of cough, blood-tinged sputum, fatigue, myalgia, shortness of breath, weight loss" -> "Possible underlying systemic inflammatory condition" -> "Further evaluation warranted" -> 80% CHAIN: "Diffuse rhonchi on chest auscultation, palpable erythematous lesions on lower extremities" -> "Possible systemic vasculitis" -> "Further evaluation indicated" -> 75% CHAIN: "Laboratory findings of leukocytosis, elevated ESR, proteinuria, hematuria, RBC casts" -> "Possible renal involvement in systemic disease" -> "Further testing needed" -> 70% CHAIN: "Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) titer, family history of systemic lupus erythematosus" -> "Possible autoimmune etiology" -> "Likelihood of positive autoimmune markers" -> 80%
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms suggestive of systemic vasculitis, likely granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis). The skin biopsy findings of arteriolar and capillary inflammation support this diagnosis. Given the clinical picture and laboratory findings, further evaluation is most likely to show myeloperoxidase antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (p-ANCA) positivity, which is commonly associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
